questions.question: In a periodic-review single-item inventory system under a base-stock policy with order-up-to level $S$, the order $Q_k$ placed at the start of period $k$ is $S$ minus which quantity?
options: The inventory level $I_{k-1}'$ at the end of period $k-1$
The inventory position $P_{k-1}'$ at the end of period $k-1$
The inventory position $P_{k-1}$ at the start of period $k-1$
The on-hand stock $(I_{k-1}')^+$ at the end of period $k-1$

questions.question: In a periodic-review single-item inventory system under a base-stock policy with order-up-to level $S$, starting from inventory position $P_1=S$ and with lead time $l\ge1$, which quantity equals $S$ at the start of every period $k$, whatever the demand sequence?
options: The inventory level $I_k$, i.e. what is on the shelf minus the backlog
The quantity on order, i.e. the orders placed but not yet received
The inventory position $P_k$, i.e. the level plus the quantity on order
The end-of-period inventory position $P_k'$, after demand $D_k$

questions.question: A periodic-review base-stock policy orders the previous period's demand at the start of each period. For which items is it a suitable policy, and why?
options: Items with a small setup cost per order, since an order is placed in almost every period
Items with a large setup cost per order, since each order is small and so cheap to place
Items with a large setup cost per order, since orders are only placed when stock runs out
Items with a small setup cost per order, since the policy never orders in two periods in a row

questions.question: A $(Q,r)$ policy orders, when the end-of-period position satisfies $P_{k-1}'\le r$, the smallest number of lots of size $Q$ that lifts the position into $\{r+1,\dots,r+Q\}$. Which choice turns it into the base-stock policy with order-up-to level $S$?
options: $Q=1$ and $r=S$
$Q=S$ and $r=0$
$Q=S$ and $r=S-1$
$Q=1$ and $r=S-1$

questions.question: Two shops face the same demand sequence and both use a base-stock policy with the same order-up-to level $S$, starting with $I_1=P_1=S$ and nothing on order. Shop A has lead time $l=1$ and shop B lead time $l=2$. How do their start-of-period inventory levels $I_k$ compare for $k\ge3$?
options: They are equal, since both inventory positions equal $S$ in every period
Shop B's level is $D_{k-2}$ lower, since $I_k=S-D_{k-2}-D_{k-1}$ there, against $S-D_{k-1}$ in shop A
Shop B's level is higher, since its orders are placed earlier and arrive in larger amounts
Shop B's level is $D_{k-1}$ lower, since shop B's orders arrive one period later than shop A's

questions.question: In a periodic-review single-item inventory system under a base-stock policy with order-up-to level $S=7$, at the end of period $k-1$ the shop has $1$ unit on the shelf, no backlog and $2$ units on order. How many units does it order at the start of period $k$?
options: $6$ units
$5$ units
$7$ units
$4$ units

questions.question: A shop orders under a base-stock policy with order-up-to level $S=6$ and lead time $l=1$. It starts with $P_1=I_1=6$ and nothing on order, and the demands are $D_1,D_2,D_3,D_4=4,1,3,2$. Which orders $Q_1,Q_2,Q_3,Q_4$ does it place?

With lead time $l=1$ and order-up-to level $S=9$, a base-stock shop started with $I_1=P_1=9$ and nothing on order. In a period $k\ge2$, last period's demand was $D_{k-1}=4$ and this period's demand will be $D_k=2$. What is the inventory level $I_k$ at the start of period $k$?

A make-to-order firm is modelled as a base-stock system with order-up-to level $S=0$ and a one-period lead time, starting from $I_1=P_1=0$ with nothing on order. If $D_{k-1}=3$ and $D_k=4$ for some $k\ge2$, what is its end-of-period inventory level $I_k'$?

Replenishments arrive instantly (lead time $l=0$) for a shop with a base-stock policy, order-up-to level $S=5$ and $I_1=P_1=5$. Given $D_{k-1}=3$ and $D_k=2$ for some $k\ge2$, how much stock, $I_k$, is on the shelf at the start of period $k$?

Two shops face the same demands $D_1,D_2,\dots$ and lead time $l=1$. Shop A uses a base-stock policy with $S=5$, shop B one with $S=9$, and each starts with $I_1=P_1=S$ and nothing on order. How do their orders $Q_k$ compare for $k\ge2$?
options: Shop B orders $4$ more units than shop A in every period
Shop B orders less often, since its higher stock lasts several periods
Shop B's orders are $\frac{9}{5}$ times those of shop A in every period
Both shops order exactly $D_{k-1}$, so their orders are identical

questions.question: In a periodic-review single-item inventory system under a base-stock policy with order-up-to level $S$ and fixed lead time $l$, starting from $I_1=P_1=S$ with nothing on order, $S$ is raised by one unit while the demand sequence stays the same. What happens to the number of periods that end without backlog ($I_k'\ge0$)?
options: It strictly increases, since every end-of-period level $I_k'$ rises by one
It is unchanged, since the extra unit stays in the pipeline and never reaches the shelf
It cannot decrease, since every $I_k'$ rises by one, but it may stay the same
It may decrease, since the higher level also raises every order $Q_k$ by one

questions.question: A shop uses a base-stock policy with order-up-to level $S\ge0$, and holding one unit on the shelf for a period costs far more than backlogging one unit of demand for a period ($h\gg b$). Which choice of $S$ fits these costs?
options: A high $S$, since a base-stock policy should keep the share of periods with backlog near zero
A low $S$ such as $S=0$, so demand waits for replenishment and almost nothing is held
$S$ equal to the largest demand in one period, so that each period's demand is covered
Any $S$ is equally good, since the orders equal the previous demand whatever $S$ is

questions.question: Orders take three periods to arrive ($l=3$) for a shop using a base-stock policy with $S=12$; it began with $I_1=P_1=12$ and nothing outstanding. For a period $k>3$ with demands $D_{k-3}=2$, $D_{k-2}=4$, $D_{k-1}=3$ and $D_k=5$, what is the start-of-period inventory level $I_k$?

A shop uses a base-stock policy with order-up-to level $S=10$, but each order may contain at most $Q=4$ units. At the end of period $k-1$ the inventory position is $P_{k-1}'=3$. What are the order $Q_k$ and the position $P_k$ at the start of period $k$?
options: $Q_k=0$ and $P_k=3$
$Q_k=4$ and $P_k=7$

questions.question: In a periodic-review single-item inventory system under a base-stock policy with order-up-to level $S=5$ and lead time $l=2$, starting from $I_1=P_1=S$ with nothing on order, the inventory level at the start of a period $k\ge3$ is $I_k=-2$, i.e. a backlog of $2$ units. How many units are on order at that moment?
options: $3$ units
$5$ units
$7$ units
$2$ units

questions.question: Under a base-stock policy with order-up-to level $S$, orders must satisfy $Q_k\ge0$, and the identity $P_k=S$ for all $k$ is derived from the start $P_1=S$. Which statement about another starting position $P_1$ is correct?
options: With $P_1>S$, the rule $Q_k=S-P_{k-1}'$ can ask for a negative order, so $P_k=S$ may fail at first
With $P_1<S$, the position may never reach $S$, since each order only replaces the previous demand
Any $P_1$ works, since the rule always restores the position to $S$ in the following period
With $P_1>S$, the rule still gives $P_k=S$, and the orders then exceed the previous demand

questions.question: In a periodic-review single-item inventory system under a base-stock policy with order-up-to level $S$, lead time $l\ge1$, $I_1=P_1=S$ and nothing on order at the start, consider periods $1,\dots,k$ with $k>l+1$. Which statement about the total ordered in periods $1,\dots,k$ and the total received by the start of period $k$ is correct?
options: Ordered: $D_1+\dots+D_k$; received: $D_1+\dots+D_{k-l}$
Ordered: $D_1+\dots+D_{k-1}$; received: $D_1+\dots+D_{k-1}$
Ordered: $D_1+\dots+D_{k-1}$; received: $D_1+\dots+D_{k-l}$
Ordered: $D_1+\dots+D_{k-1}$; received: $D_1+\dots+D_{k-l-1}$

questions.question: In a periodic-review single-item inventory system under a base-stock policy with order-up-to level $S$ and lead time $l=2$, starting from $I_1=P_1=S$ with nothing on order, the demand in every period is an integer between $0$ and $5$. What is the smallest $S$ that guarantees $I_k'\ge0$ (no backlog at the end of any period) for every possible demand sequence?

A shop starts period $1$ with $I_1=6$ units on the shelf and $3$ units on order. It orders nothing in period $1$ and afterwards always orders the previous period's demand, $Q_k=D_{k-1}$ for $k\ge2$. Which policy is this?
options: The base-stock policy with $S=6$, the stock on the shelf at the start
The base-stock policy with $S=9$, the starting inventory position
No base-stock policy, since the shelf level $I_k$ changes from period to period
No base-stock policy, since units ordered before period $1$ break the rule $Q_k=S-P_{k-1}'$
